react-native-basics/1/1.title: Welcome to the course
react-native-basics/1/1.body:
In this lesson, you will learn what React Native is, how it renders mobile user interfaces, and how its Core Components map directly to native building blocks on Android and iOS.

## What is React Native?

React Native is an open source framework for creating Android and iOS applications using React and the native capabilities of mobile platforms. Instead of writing separate applications in platform languages such as Swift or Kotlin, you write JavaScript to describe your user interface and interact with platform APIs.

Your interface is defined using React components: reusable, nestable bundles of code that describe both appearance and behaviour.

## Views and Native Components

In Android and iOS development, the fundamental building block of an interface is a **view**. Each view represents a rectangular screen area that presents content such as text or pictures, or handles user interactions. Every visual detail on screen, including buttons and single lines of text, is formed by views, and views can be nested within one another to build complex layouts.

Native engineers construct these elements with Kotlin or Java on Android, and Swift or Objective-C on iOS. React Native lets you orchestrate those same elements through JavaScript by declaring React components. When the application executes, the framework produces the genuine platform views that match those declarations. Because your UI is backed by standard mobile platform views, the application retains the exact appearance, tactile feel, and performance of native software. Components connected to platform views in this way are known as **Native Components**.

## Core Components

React Native provides a collection of essential, ready-to-use Native Components known as **Core Components**. When building an interface, you will work frequently with these primary components:

- `<View>`: A non-scrolling container that supports layout with flexbox, style, touch handling, and accessibility controls (corresponding to Android `<ViewGroup>` and iOS `<UIView>`).
- `<Text>`: Displays, styles, and nests strings of text, and can handle touch events (corresponding to Android `<TextView>` and iOS `<UITextView>`).
- `<Image>`: Displays different types of images (corresponding to Android `<ImageView>` and iOS `<UIImageView>`).
- `<ScrollView>`: A generic scrolling container that can contain multiple components and views (corresponding to Android `<ScrollView>` and iOS `<UIScrollView>`).
- `<TextInput>`: Allows the user to enter text (corresponding to Android `<EditText>` and iOS `<UITextField>`).

Here is a short example in `App.tsx` demonstrating how Core Components nest together:

```tsx
import React from 'react';
import { View, Text, Image, TextInput, ScrollView } from 'react-native';

const App = (): React.JSX.Element => {
  return (
    <ScrollView>
      <Text>Welcome to React Native</Text>
      <View>
        <Image
          source={{ uri: 'https://reactnative.dev/docs/assets/p_cat2.png' }}
          style={{ width: 200, height: 200 }}
        />
      </View>
      <TextInput
        defaultValue="You can type in me"
        style={{ height: 40, borderColor: 'gray', borderWidth: 1 }}
      />
    </ScrollView>
  );
};

export default App;
```

### Try it

Look closely at the code example above. Note how `<ScrollView>` wraps the rest of the elements to provide scrolling, while `<View>` acts as a container for `<Image>`. Try identifying which native view would be created on iOS for `<TextInput>` and which would be created on Android for `<Text>`.

### Key points

- React Native is an open source framework that lets you build native Android and iOS apps using JavaScript and React.
- Mobile user interfaces are built from rectangular building blocks called views, which can be nested inside other views.
- React Native components map directly to native Android and iOS views at runtime, preserving native look and performance.
- Common Core Components include `<View>`, `<Text>`, `<Image>`, `<ScrollView>`, and `<TextInput>`.

react-native-basics/1/2.title: Setting up Expo
react-native-basics/1/2.body:
In this lesson, you will prepare your machine and initialise a new Expo project for React Native development.

## Checking your system requirements

Before creating an app, you need to ensure your computer has the necessary prerequisites installed.

Expo requires the LTS release of Node.js. It supports the following operating systems:

- macOS
- Windows (using PowerShell or WSL 2)
- Linux

You can run setup commands with package managers such as `npm` (via `npx`), `yarn`, `pnpm`, or `bun`.

## Creating a default project

Expo is a React Native framework designed to simplify mobile development on Android and iOS. It provides file-based routing and a standard library of native modules.

To create a new project, Expo recommends starting with the default project created by the `create-expo-app` utility. You can generate a default project targeting SDK 58 by running:

```bash
npx create-expo-app@latest --template default@sdk-58
```

This default project sets up a ready-to-run structure containing example code to guide you. In this course, examples use TypeScript. If you prefer another package manager, you can run an equivalent command, such as:

```bash
yarn create expo-app --template default@sdk-58
```

You can also use `pnpm create expo-app --template default@sdk-58` or `bun create expo --template default@sdk-58`.

If you prefer to explore specific features instead of the default project, you can pass the `--example` flag to browse available sample applications:

```bash
npx create-expo-app@latest --example
```

You can also provide an example name directly, such as:

```bash
npx create-expo-app@latest --example with-widgets
```

## Choosing how to develop

When setting up your environment, you have two primary options for running your app:

- **Expo Go**: A playground designed for students and learners to try Expo quickly.
- **Development build**: A build of your own app that includes Expo's developer tools.

Expo recommends developing on a real device so you can see exactly what your users will experience. However, note that during the SDK 58 transition period, if you plan to use Expo Go on a physical device, you must use an SDK 57 project instead. Running `create-expo-app@latest` without the `--template` flag creates an SDK 57 project for this purpose.

### Try it

Open your terminal and create a new Expo project using the default SDK 58 template:

```bash
npx create-expo-app@latest --template default@sdk-58
```

Once the command finishes, navigate into your new project directory and inspect the files created for your app.

### Key points

- Expo requires Node.js (LTS) on macOS, Windows (PowerShell or WSL 2), or Linux.
- You can initialise a project using `npx create-expo-app@latest --template default@sdk-58`.
- Ready-made example projects demonstrating specific features can be selected using the `--example` flag.
- Expo Go acts as a playground for quick testing, whereas a development build is a custom build of your app with Expo developer tools.
- If you plan to use Expo Go on a physical device during the SDK 58 transition period, you must use an SDK 57 project.

react-native-basics/1/3.title: Running on your phone
react-native-basics/1/3.body:
In this lesson, you will learn how to run your React Native application on a physical mobile device, establish a connection with your local development server, and view live updates as you edit your code.

## Starting the server and scanning the code

To view your project on a physical handset, you must first launch the local development server from your terminal. Navigate to your project directory and run:

```bash
npx expo start
```

Once the command executes, Expo CLI displays a QR code directly in your terminal. Scan this QR code to open the app on your device.

If you are instead developing on an Android emulator or iOS simulator, you can press `A` or `I` respectively in the terminal to open the application.

## Network configuration and account requirements

For the development server to communicate with your device, both your computer and your phone must be connected to the same Wi-Fi network.

If you are using Expo Go on a physical iOS device, Expo Go opens your project only when Expo CLI and Expo Go are signed in to the same Expo account. To log in on your computer, run:

```bash
npx expo login
```

After signing in on your computer, open Expo Go on your iOS device, tap the account icon in the top-right corner, and sign in using the identical account.

If your device still cannot connect, it may be due to router configuration, which is common on public networks. You can work around this by choosing the tunnel connection type when starting the development server:

```bash
npx expo start --tunnel
```

Scan the QR code again after starting the server with this flag. Keep in mind that using the tunnel connection type makes app reloads considerably slower than on LAN or Local, so it is best to avoid tunnel when possible.

## Testing changes with Fast Refresh

Expo Go is configured by default to reload the app automatically whenever a file is changed. To see this in action, open `src/app/index.tsx` in your code editor and update the welcome heading:

```tsx
export default function HomeScreen(): React.JSX.Element {
  return (
    <ThemedView style={styles.heroSection}>
      <AnimatedIcon />
      <ThemedText type="title" style={styles.title}>
        Hello World!
      </ThemedText>
    </ThemedView>
  );
}
```

Once you save the file, the app reloads so that your JavaScript and component changes appear immediately on your device.

If updates do not appear automatically on your screen, verify that development mode is enabled in Expo CLI. You can also close and reopen the Expo app, then shake your physical device to open the developer menu. If Fast Refresh is enabled, toggle it; if you see Disable Fast Refresh, dismiss the developer menu and make another change to test the connection.

### Try it

1. Run `npx expo start` in your project terminal.
2. Scan the displayed QR code to open the app on your handset.
3. Open `src/app/index.tsx`, change the title text to `Hello World!`, and save the file.
4. Check that the screen automatically reloads with the new text, then shake the device to inspect the developer menu.

### Key points

- Start the local development server with `npx expo start` and scan the terminal QR code to open the app on your device.
- Ensure your computer and device share the same Wi-Fi network.
- Physical iOS devices require Expo CLI and Expo Go to be signed in to the same Expo account.
- Use `npx expo start --tunnel` if router configuration on public networks prevents a direct connection.
- Shake your physical device to reveal the developer menu and verify Fast Refresh settings.

react-native-basics/2/1.title: Views, text and images
react-native-basics/2/1.body:
In this lesson, you will learn how to structure mobile screens using three fundamental React Native components: `View`, `Text`, and `Image`. You will see how these components map to native interfaces and how to configure their properties properly.

## Structuring screens with `View`
The `View` component is the most fundamental building block in React Native. It functions as a container that maps directly to native view equivalents, such as `UIView` on iOS or `android.view` on Android.

You use `View` to organise your user interface into rectangular sections, arrange children, and group items. A `View` can contain zero, one, or many child components of any kind.

```tsx
<View style={{padding: 16, backgroundColor: '#f0f0f0'}}>
  <View style={{height: 50, backgroundColor: 'blue'}} />
  <View style={{height: 50, backgroundColor: 'red'}} />
</View>
```

## Rendering text with `Text`
Unlike web development where text can be placed directly inside any container, React Native is strict: you must always wrap all text strings inside a `<Text>` component. Placing a raw text string directly under a `<View>` will raise an exception.

The `<Text>` component uses text layout rather than flexbox layout for its children. When you nest `Text` elements inside an outer `Text` component, the nested elements flow inline and wrap together at the end of a line instead of forming separate rectangular boxes. Nested text also inherits styles from its parent text container.

You can control how long passages overflow by providing the `numberOfLines` prop, which truncates excess content with an ellipsis:

```tsx
<View>
  <Text style={{fontSize: 16, color: 'black'}}>
    Welcome back,{' '}
    <Text style={{fontWeight: 'bold', color: 'blue'}}>Alex</Text>
  </Text>
  <Text numberOfLines={2}>
    This is a longer paragraph that will automatically truncate if it exceeds two lines of text on the screen.
  </Text>
</View>
```

## Loading images with `Image`
The `Image` component displays pictures from local assets or remote URLs. React Native handles each type of source differently:

1. **Static local images**: You reference local files using `require('./path/to/image.png')`. Metro resolves these at build time, and the bundler automatically detects image dimensions. You can provide `@2x` and `@3x` suffixes in your file names, and the bundler will select the correct density variant for the device screen.
2. **Network images**: Remote images take an object with a `uri` string, such as `source={{uri: 'https://reactjs.org/logo-og.png'}}`. Because remote dimensions are not known before download, you must manually specify `width` and `height` in the style. If you omit these dimensions, the image will not display.

Here is an example combining these three components in `ProfileCard.tsx`:

```tsx
import {View, Text, Image, StyleSheet} from 'react-native';

type ProfileCardProps = {
  version: string;
  description: string;
};

export default function ProfileCard({version, description}: ProfileCardProps) {
  return (
    <View style={styles.card}>
      <Image
        source={{uri: 'https://reactjs.org/logo-og.png'}}
        style={styles.avatar}
      />
      <Text style={styles.title}>
        React Native <Text style={{fontWeight: 'bold'}}>{version}</Text>
      </Text>
      <Text numberOfLines={1}>{description}</Text>
    </View>
  );
}

const styles = StyleSheet.create({
  card: {padding: 16, backgroundColor: '#ffffff'},
  avatar: {width: 60, height: 60},
  title: {fontSize: 18},
});
```

### Try it
Create a card component that renders an outer `View` container with padding. Inside it, render a remote `Image` with an explicit `width` and `height` of 80, followed by a `Text` element showing a title and a nested `Text` element displaying a badge in bold.

### Key points
- `View` is the core layout container and maps directly to native platform equivalents like `UIView` and `android.view`.
- All text strings must be wrapped inside a `Text` component; placing raw text directly inside a `View` raises an exception.
- Nested `Text` components use inline text layout rather than flexbox, and inherit styles from the parent `Text` component.
- Local images loaded via `require` automatically supply their dimensions, whereas remote images loaded using `{uri: ...}` require explicit `width` and `height` styles.

ui-design-fundamentals/1/1.title: What makes a good interface
ui-design-fundamentals/1/1.body:
In this lesson, you will learn how to evaluate what makes a digital interface effective, usable, and trustworthy. Great interfaces are not merely visually polished; they solve real problems, respect user constraints, and make complex tasks feel effortless.

## Starting with real user needs

A good interface begins with the person using it, not the internal preferences of the team building it. When you design an interface, you must identify your primary audience, their practical goals, and the emotional, physical, and technical contexts in which they operate.

Interfaces often fail when designers rely on personal assumptions rather than observed behaviour. In design frameworks like the NHS Service Manual and the U.S. Web Design System (USWDS), strong design requires you to:

- **Understand the outcome**: Focus on what the user wants to achieve and how measurable outcomes improve lives.
- **Do the hard work to make it simple**: Tackle underlying complexities instead of passing confusing steps onto the user.
- **Test your assumptions**: Put early prototypes in front of real people, observing where they hesitate, stumble, or succeed rather than relying on hunches.

## Inclusion and accessibility from day one

Accessibility is not an optional extra or a checklist item reserved for the end of a project. An interface is only effective if it can be navigated by the broadest possible audience, including individuals using screen readers, keyboard-only navigation, or those with varied cognitive and physical needs.

Embracing accessibility means designing generously and treating accessibility standards as helpful design constraints. In practice, this requires clear colour contrast, logical heading structures, and interactive elements with distinct, accurately labelled targets. Clear plain language also ensures that people who skim and scan can quickly absorb essential information without struggling through dense jargon.

## Designing for trust and continuity

Trust must be earned through reliable behaviour, honesty, and transparent feedback. When an interface crashes, fails to protect private data, or leaves people uncertain about what happens next, trust is eroded. Reducing the impact of failure with resilient engineering, continuous testing, and simple error handling keeps experiences dependable.

Promoting continuity means creating consistent experiences across journeys, devices, and sessions. A well-designed workflow helps users understand where they are at each step and what to expect next. For example, in a multi-step service:

- **Clarify the process**: Give users unambiguous guidance about their current step and the actions needed to move forward.
- **Support multi-session tasks**: Allow people to save their progress, exit safely, and return later without starting over.
- **Enable safe corrections**: Ensure users can review their entries, edit submitted data, or undo actions before completing a workflow.

### Try it

Open a public or everyday service you use regularly, such as a health appointment service or an online banking portal. Review one multi-step workflow against three criteria:

1. Does the interface clearly tell you what step you are on and what will happen next?
2. Can you easily scan the text in plain language, or is complexity pushed onto you?
3. What happens if you make an error or need to step away—can you undo actions and resume your session safely?

### Key points

- Put people at the centre by addressing real user needs rather than designing around assumptions.
- Do the hard work behind the scenes so the interface remains simple and clear for the user.
- Build accessibility into every decision from the start so anyone can engage with the service.
- Earn trust by offering reliable performance, clear language, and predictable continuity across tasks.

ui-design-fundamentals/2/2.body:
In this lesson, you will learn how a type scale organises font sizes and line heights across an interface, why consistent vertical rhythm aids readability, and how type adapts responsively to smaller screens.

## What is a type scale?

A type scale is a curated collection of font sizes and matching line heights that underpins every typographic style in a user interface. Rather than choosing arbitrary sizes for each heading or paragraph, you select points from a shared scale.

A core principle of a type scale is maintaining vertical rhythm. In the GOV.UK Design System, every step on the scale pairs a font size with a line height calculated in a multiple of 5px. This strict multiple helps text align smoothly down the page, making layouts structured, balanced, and easier for users to scan.

While design documentation often displays values in pixels (`px`) for clarity, production stylesheets typically output relative units such as `rem` or `em`. Relative units ensure that text scales appropriately whenever users zoom in or adjust their browser display settings.

## Responsive type behaviour

Text needs to look clear and well proportioned whether viewed on a desktop monitor or a mobile device. A responsive type scale adjusts font sizes and line heights according to screen width.

In this system, the large screen scale activates once the screen exceeds the 640px tablet breakpoint:

- Point 48 (extra-large heading): 48px font size with a 50px line height on large screens, shifting down to 32px font size with a 35px line height on small screens.
- Point 36 (large heading): 36px font size with a 40px line height on large screens, reducing to 27px font size with a 30px line height on small screens.
- Point 24 (medium heading or large body): 24px font size with a 30px line height on large screens, adjusting to 21px font size with a 25px line height on small screens.
- Point 19 (small heading or standard body): 19px font size with a 25px line height across all screen sizes.
- Point 16 (smaller body text): 16px font size with a 20px line height across all screen sizes.

Notice how body text at points 16 and 19 remains constant across device sizes to preserve readability, while larger display headings scale down to avoid dominating narrow mobile viewports.

## Implementing the scale

When working in Sass, mixins apply the predetermined sizes and line heights directly to UI elements:

```css
/* Apply font size and line height only */
@include govuk-font-size($size: 19);

/* Apply font size, line height, and font family styling */
@include govuk-font($size: 19, $weight: bold);
```

Using `govuk-font-size` updates just the font size and matching line height. In contrast, `govuk-font` also applies typographic properties such as the New Transport font family and weight parameters.

### Try it

Choose three points on the scale: one for an extra-large heading, one for standard body text, and one for smaller body text. Write down the corresponding font size and line height for both large and small screens. Check that each line height is an exact multiple of 5px.

### Key points

- A type scale provides a consistent set of font sizes and paired line heights for all typographic elements.
- Using line heights in multiples of 5px establishes a predictable vertical rhythm that improves reading flow.
- Headings scale down on viewports below the 640px tablet breakpoint, whereas core body sizes remain constant.
- Relative units like `rem` and `em` allow text to scale smoothly when users zoom or magnify their screens.
- Dedicated Sass mixins let you apply scale points directly, either as standalone sizes or paired with font families.

python-for-everyone/1/1.title: Why Python?
python-for-everyone/1/1.body:
In this lesson, you will discover what Python is, why developers choose it for everyday tasks, and how its design helps you write clear and compact programs.

## Solving everyday problems

When working on computers, you often encounter repetitive chores that you would like to automate. You might need to carry out a search-and-replace operation across dozens of text files, or rename and reorganise a collection of photo files. You may also want to build a small custom database, a simple game, or a specialised graphical user interface (GUI) application.

You could write Unix shell scripts or Windows batch files for some of these jobs. However, shell scripts are best suited to moving files and modifying text data; they are not well suited to writing games or GUI applications. On the other hand, traditional compiled languages such as C, C++, or Java require significant development time before you can produce even a first draft. Python bridges this gap: it is simpler to use than compiled languages, runs across Windows, macOS, and Unix systems, and provides the structure needed for larger programs.

## A very-high-level, interpreted language

Python is a real programming language that offers much more structure than simple scripts, along with built-in error checking and powerful high-level data types such as flexible arrays and dictionaries. These general-purpose types allow you to carry out complex operations in a single statement, making Python applicable to a wide range of tasks.

Python is also an interpreted language. Because there is no separate compilation and linking step, you avoid the slow write-compile-test cycle found in C or Java. You can run Python interactively, allowing you to experiment with language features, test individual functions, and even use the interpreter as a handy desk calculator.

## Clean syntax and modular design

Programs written in Python are usually substantially shorter and more readable than equivalent programs in C or Java. This brevity comes from three design choices:

- High-level data types let you express complex actions concisely.
- Statement grouping relies on indentation rather than beginning and ending brackets.
- You do not need to write variable or argument declarations.

Here is a short example demonstrating how Python groups statements using indentation without needing variable type declarations or curly brackets:

```python
file_count = 12
if file_count > 10:
    action = "batch rename"
    ready = True
```

Python also allows you to split code into reusable modules. It includes a comprehensive collection of standard modules providing file I/O, system calls, sockets, and interfaces for GUI toolkits like Tk. If needed, Python is extensible, meaning you can hook C libraries into Python or embed the Python interpreter into larger applications.

Finally, the language takes its name from the BBC television comedy series "Monty Python's Flying Circus", not from reptiles.

### Try it

Think of a repetitive task on your computer that you currently perform by hand, such as sorting through downloaded files or editing text files. Consider which features of Python—such as built-in file handling modules or high-level data types—make it better suited for that task than a shell script or a compiled language.

### Key points

- Python is an interpreted language that removes the slow compile-and-link cycle, allowing interactive testing and quick development.
- Programs are compact and readable because statement grouping uses indentation rather than brackets, and variable declarations are not required.
- Python includes high-level built-in data types, such as flexible arrays and dictionaries, alongside standard modules for file I/O, networking, and GUIs.
- The language is named after the BBC comedy show "Monty Python's Flying Circus".

python-for-everyone/1/2.title: Installing Python
python-for-everyone/1/2.body:
In this lesson, you will learn how to install Python on Windows and macOS using the official tools provided by the Python team, and how to verify that your installation is ready to use.

## Installing on Windows

Unlike many Unix-based systems, Windows does not come with a system installation of Python. The official method to set up Python on Windows is using the Python install manager. You can obtain it either by downloading the installer from `python.org/downloads` or directly through the Microsoft Store app.

Once the install manager is set up, several global commands become available in your terminal or PowerShell:

- `python`: Launches your current latest version of Python.
- `py`: The versatile launcher command that can run scripts, select specific versions, and manage installations.
- `pymanager`: An unambiguous command for managing Python installations.

If you run `python` or `py` when no runtime versions are installed yet, the install manager can automatically download and install the current release for you. You can also view or add runtimes directly from your terminal:

```bash
py list --online
py install default
```

## Installing on macOS

For macOS, the Python release team provides a standard installer package (`.pkg`) downloadable from `python.org/downloads`. Current installers provide a universal binary build that runs natively on both Apple Silicon and Intel Macs.

To install Python on macOS:

1. Download the `.pkg` installer file from the official website and double-click it to start the installer application.
2. Step through the **Read Me** and click **Agree** to accept the licence terms.
3. Complete the installation steps. An administrator username and password will be requested.
4. Once the installer finishes, locate the new Python folder created inside your `Applications` folder.
5. Double-click the `Install Certificates.command` file inside that folder. This opens a terminal window to download and set up SSL root certificates required for secure connections.

A default macOS installation places the Python framework in `/Library/Frameworks/Python.framework`, adds shortcuts in `/usr/local/bin/`, and includes the IDLE development environment in your `Applications` folder.

## Verifying your installation

After completing the installation on either platform, open a fresh terminal window (PowerShell or Command Prompt on Windows, Terminal on macOS) and run the interpreter to verify that Python starts:

On Windows:

```bash
py
```

On macOS:

```bash
python3
```

If the command opens an interactive prompt displaying the Python version information, your installation is working properly.

### Try it

Open your terminal or command prompt and test that your installation is working. On Windows, type `py list` to view your installed runtimes. On macOS, type `python3 -VV` to check the installed Python version and build details. Exit any open Python session by closing the terminal window.

### Key points

- On Windows, install the Python install manager from python.org or the Microsoft Store to access the `python` and `py` commands.
- On macOS, download and run the `.pkg` installer package from python.org.
- On macOS, always double-click `Install Certificates.command` in the Applications folder after installing to configure SSL certificates.
- Launch the interactive Python environment by running `py` on Windows or `python3` on macOS in your terminal.

python-for-everyone/1/3.body:
In this lesson, you will run your first Python commands to display output on the screen. You will learn how to start the interactive interpreter, work with strings and the `print()` function, and add comments to your code.

## Starting the interpreter

To begin running Python commands, you can start the interpreter in interactive mode. In a Unix shell, you launch it by typing the command:

```bash
python3.15
```

On Windows machines where the Python launcher is installed, you can run `py`. When interactive mode begins, the interpreter prints a welcome message showing its version number and a copyright notice before presenting the primary prompt, which is usually three greater-than signs (`>>>`).

The `>>>` prompt indicates that Python is waiting for your instructions. When you want to leave the interpreter, you can type `quit()` at the prompt, or enter an end-of-file character by pressing Control-D on Unix (Control-Z on Windows).

## Writing your first program

You can display output in Python using the built-in `print()` function. For example, you can print a message directly:

```python
>>> print("Be careful not to fall off!")
Be careful not to fall off!
```

Text in Python is represented by strings of type `str`. You define a string literal by enclosing characters in either single quotes (`'...'`) or double quotes (`"..."`) with the same result:

```python
>>> 'spam eggs'
'spam eggs'
>>> "Paris rabbit got your back :)! Yay!"
'Paris rabbit got your back :)! Yay!'
```

When you enter a string directly at the prompt without `print()`, the interpreter displays it with its enclosing quotes. The `print()` function produces cleaner, more readable output by omitting the quotes and interpreting special characters:

```python
>>> s = 'First line.\nSecond line.'
>>> print(s)
First line.
Second line.
```

The `print()` function also handles multiple arguments. It inserts a space between items, which lets you combine text and expressions:

```python
>>> i = 256 * 256
>>> print('The value of i is', i)
The value of i is 65536
```

## Adding comments to your code

As you write code, you will often want to include comments to clarify what the program does. In Python, comments begin with the hash character (`#`) and run to the end of the physical line:

```python
# this is the first comment
spam = 1  # and this is the second comment
          # ... and now a third!
```

Python ignores comments completely when executing code. A comment can appear at the start of a line or after whitespace or code, but not inside a string literal. A hash character placed inside quotation marks is simply treated as part of the text:

```python
>>> text = "# This is not a comment because it's inside quotes."
```

## Running a command from the terminal

Besides entering commands interactively line by line, you can pass a command directly to the interpreter from your shell using the `-c` option:

```bash
python3.15 -c "print('The value of i is', 256 * 256)"
```

Because Python statements frequently contain quotation marks and spaces that might confuse your system shell, it is best to quote the entire command argument.

### Try it

Open your terminal or command prompt, start the Python interpreter by typing `python3.15` (or `py` on Windows), and wait for the `>>>` prompt. Type `print("Be careful not to fall off!")`, press Return to run it, and then exit the interpreter by typing `quit()`.

### Key points

- The interactive interpreter displays the `>>>` primary prompt when ready for input.
- Text strings can be enclosed in either single (`'...'`) or double (`"..."`) quotation marks with identical results.
- The `print()` function writes its arguments without enclosing quotes and automatically separates multiple items with spaces.
- Comments begin with `#`, extend to the end of the physical line, and are ignored by Python.
- You can exit the interpreter by typing `quit()` or by pressing Control-D on Unix (Control-Z on Windows).

python-for-everyone/1/4.body:
In this lesson, you will learn how to create variables, follow Python's naming conventions, and distinguish between fundamental data types such as integers, floating-point numbers, and strings.

## Assigning values to variables

A variable allows a program to store a value under a friendly name rather than a raw memory location. You assign a value to a variable using the assignment operator (`=`). The left-hand side specifies the variable name, whilst the right-hand side provides the value or calculation to store.

```python
width = 20
height = 5 * 9
area = width * height
print(area)
```

Unlike mathematical equality, an assignment statement assigns or updates a value. A variable begins to exist only when you assign it for the first time. If you try to refer to a variable that has not been defined, Python stops and raises a `NameError`.

## Naming rules for variables

When choosing names for variables, you must follow Python's syntax rules:

- Names can contain letters, digits, and underscores, but they must not start with a digit (for example, `101class` is invalid).
- Variable names are case-sensitive, which means `Total`, `total`, and `TOTAL` are completely separate variables.
- You cannot use reserved keywords (such as `if`, `while`, `def`, or `class`) as variable names.

Python's style guide recommends using snake case for variable names, which means writing all characters in lowercase and separating words with underscores, such as `first_name` or `total_price`.

## Working with fundamental types

Every value in Python has a data type that determines how the interpreter represents and handles it. The three basic types you will encounter most often are:

- **Integers (`int`)**: whole numbers without decimals, such as `2` or `-42`.
- **Floating-point numbers (`float`)**: numbers that include a fractional part, such as `10.5` or `3.14`. Dividing two numbers with the `/` operator always returns a float.
- **Strings (`str`)**: sequences of text wrapped in matching single (`'`) or double (`"`) quotes, such as `'Liverpool'` or `"Hello, World!"`.

You can inspect the data type of any value using the built-in `type()` function:

```python
item_count = 5
item_price = 2.50
store_name = "Bakery"

print(type(item_count))
print(type(item_price))
print(type(store_name))
```

### Key points

- The assignment operator (`=`) binds a value to a variable name.
- Variable names cannot begin with digits or use reserved language keywords.
- Python distinguishes between upper and lower case letters in variable names.
- Integers represent whole numbers, floats represent numbers with decimals, and strings represent text.
- The `type()` function identifies the data type of any variable or literal value.

python-for-everyone/2/1.body:
In this lesson, you will learn how to make decisions in your code using Python's `if`, `elif`, and `else` statements. By testing conditions, you can control which blocks of code execute based on the data your program receives.

## The basic if statement

The most familiar tool for controlling program flow is the `if` statement. It evaluates an expression, and if that expression is true, it runs the indented code directly below it.

```python
x = int(input("Please enter an integer: "))

if x < 0:
    x = 0
    print("Negative changed to zero")
```

In Python, indentation defines which statements belong inside a conditional block. The standard convention is to use four spaces for each indentation level. If the condition `x < 0` is false, Python skips the indented block and continues running the rest of the script.

## Handling multiple branches with elif

When you need to test several mutually exclusive conditions, you can add `elif` clauses. The keyword `elif` is short for 'else if'. Using `elif` keeps your code tidy and avoids the excessive indentation that nested `if` statements would create.

```python
x = 1

if x == 0:
    print("Zero")
elif x == 1:
    print("Single")
```

You can chain zero or more `elif` statements after an initial `if`. Python evaluates each condition from top to bottom. As soon as one condition evaluates to true, Python executes that branch and skips all remaining `elif` checks. This behaviour makes an `if ... elif ... elif ...` sequence a practical substitute for `switch` or `case` constructs found in other programming languages.

## Catch-all fallback with else

You can provide a fallback block using an `else` statement at the very end of your sequence. The `else` clause is completely optional. It executes only when the leading `if` and all subsequent `elif` conditions have evaluated to false.

```python
x = 42

if x < 0:
    print("Negative")
elif x == 0:
    print("Zero")
elif x == 1:
    print("Single")
else:
    print("More")
```

In this example, since `42` is not less than 0, not equal to 0, and not equal to 1, Python enters the `else` block and prints `More`.

### Try it

Write a short Python snippet that sets a variable `n = 0`. Use an `if`, `elif`, and `else` structure to check whether `n` is negative (`n < 0`), zero (`n == 0`), or positive. Print an appropriate message for each case.

### Key points

- The `if` statement tests a condition and executes an indented code block if that condition is true.
- You can include zero or more `elif` clauses to evaluate additional conditions without excessive indentation.
- The `else` clause is optional and runs only if none of the preceding conditions were met.
- Python relies on indentation, conventionally four spaces, to group the statements inside each conditional branch.

python-for-everyone/2/2.body:
By the end of this lesson, you will be able to repeat tasks in Python using `for` and `while` loops, generate number sequences with `range()`, and alter loop flow with `break`, `continue`, and `else`.

## Iterating with `for` and `range`

In Python, the `for` statement steps through the items of any sequence, such as a list or a string, in the order in which the items appear:

```python
words = ["apple", "banana", "cherry"]
for word in words:
    print(word, len(word))
```

When you need to iterate over a sequence of numbers, use the built-in `range()` function. It generates arithmetic progressions where the specified endpoint is never part of the sequence:

```python
for i in range(5):
    print(i)
```

This prints `0`, `1`, `2`, `3`, and `4`. You can optionally supply a starting number and a different step increment or decrement:

```python
# Prints 5, 7, and 9
for number in range(5, 10, 2):
    print(number)
```

The object returned by `range()` is iterable. Rather than constructing a full list in memory, it yields successive items on demand, saving space.

## Repeating with `while` loops

Python also provides the `while` statement to execute code repeatedly. For example, you can calculate and print numbers up to a specified boundary:

```python
a, b = 0, 1
while a < 10:
    print(a, end=" ")
    a, b = b, a + b
```

The loop executes until its condition evaluates to false. If a statement is required syntactically but no action is needed, Python provides `pass`, which can serve as a body inside a `while` loop:

```python
while True:
    pass  # Busy-wait for keyboard interrupt (Ctrl+C)
```

## Altering flow with `break`, `continue`, and `else`

You can fine-tune loop behaviour with control statements:
- `break` exits the innermost enclosing `for` or `while` loop immediately.
- `continue` skips the rest of the current iteration and advances straight to the next cycle.

```python
for num in range(2, 8):
    if num % 2 == 0:
        print(f"Found even: {num}")
        continue
    if num > 5:
        print("Exceeded limit, breaking")
        break
    print(f"Found odd: {num}")
```

Loops can also include an `else` clause. In a `for` loop, the `else` block executes after the final iteration, while in a `while` loop, it executes after the loop's condition becomes false. In either loop, Python skips the `else` block if a `break` terminates the loop early:

```python
for n in range(2, 5):
    if n == 10:
        break
else:
    print("Loop finished without breaking")
```

### Try it

Write a `for` loop using `range(1, 10)` that prints every number. Add an `if` check that uses `continue` to skip printing `5`. Finally, add an `else` block to the loop that prints `"All done!"`.

### Key points

- Python's `for` statement iterates across items of any sequence in the order they appear.
- The `range()` function generates an iterable arithmetic progression that excludes the endpoint.
- The `break` statement exits the innermost enclosing `for` or `while` loop, whereas `continue` moves to the next iteration.
- An `else` clause on a loop executes only if the loop finishes without encountering a `break`, such as when a `while` condition becomes false.

python-for-everyone/2/3.body:
You will learn how to store collections of data using lists and dictionaries, modify their contents, and inspect their elements.

## Working with lists

A list is an ordered, mutable collection of items enclosed in square brackets. Because lists are mutable, you can change their contents after creating them.

Python provides several built-in methods to modify lists:
- `append(value)` adds a new item to the end of the list.
- `remove(value)` searches for and removes the first occurrence of that value. If the item is not present, it raises a `ValueError`.
- `pop()` removes and returns the last item in the list.
- `sort()` arranges list elements in ascending order in place.
- `reverse()` reverses the elements of the list in place.

```python
fruits = ["orange", "apple", "banana"]
fruits.append("kiwi")
fruits.remove("orange")
fruits.sort()
last_fruit = fruits.pop()
print(fruits)
print(last_fruit)
```

## Working with dictionaries

A dictionary is a container that stores data in key-value pairs enclosed in curly braces `{}`. Each key is separated from its associated value by a colon, and pairs are separated by commas. Keys must be unique and immutable, such as strings or numbers, whereas values can be any object.

You can access a dictionary value using square bracket notation with the key, such as `my_dict["key"]`. If the key does not exist, Python raises a `KeyError`. To avoid this error, you can use the `get()` method, which returns `None` (or a specified fallback value) if the key is missing.

To add or modify an entry, assign a value to a key using square brackets. If the key already exists, its previous value is replaced. To remove a key-value pair, use the `del` statement or the `pop()` method:

```python
prices = {"apple": 2, "banana": 3}
prices["orange"] = 4
prices["apple"] = 1

print(prices.get("banana"))
print(prices.get("melon", 0))

del prices["orange"]
removed_price = prices.pop("banana")
print(prices)
```

## Checking membership and iterating

You can use the `in` operator to test whether a value exists in a collection. When used with a dictionary, `in` checks whether a given key exists.

You can also iterate across both data structures with a `for` loop. When looping over a dictionary directly, Python retrieves each key. To retrieve keys and values simultaneously, call the `items()` method:

```python
stock = {"apple": 10, "banana": 5}

if "apple" in stock:
    print("Apples are in stock")

for fruit, count in stock.items():
    print(fruit, count)
```

### Try it

1. Create a list called `groceries` with three food names, then add a fourth item using `append()`.
2. Create a dictionary called `prices` containing each item from your list as a key and a number as its price.
3. Use `get()` to look up the price of one item, and print the result.

### Key points

- Lists are ordered, mutable sequences modified with methods like `append()`, `remove()`, and `pop()`.
- Dictionaries store unique, immutable keys associated with values using `{key: value}` syntax.
- Look up dictionary values using square brackets or the safer `get()` method to avoid a `KeyError`.
- Use the `in` operator for membership testing and `.items()` to loop through dictionary key-value pairs.

python-for-everyone/3/1.body:
In this lesson, you will learn how to create your own reusable blocks of code in Python. You will be able to define functions that accept parameters, return results, provide default values, and use docstrings to document your code.

## Defining a basic function

In Python, you define a function using the `def` keyword, followed by the function name, a pair of parentheses, and a colon. The body of the function begins on the next line and must be indented. Good practice is to place an optional string literal on the very first line of the function body; this is known as a docstring, and it describes what the function does.

```python
def greet(name):
    """Print a greeting to the specified name."""
    print(f"Hello, {name}!")

greet("Alice")
```

When Python encounters the function call `greet("Alice")`, control flow moves into the function body, executes the indented statements, and then returns to the calling code.

## Returning values

A function can calculate a value and pass it back to the caller using the `return` statement. When Python executes a `return` statement, the function immediately terminates, and control flow hands the resulting value back to where the function was called.

```python
def calc_rectangle_area(width, height):
    """Return the area of a rectangle."""
    return width * height

area = calc_rectangle_area(5, 4)
print(area)
```

If a function reaches the end of its body without hitting a `return` statement, or if it executes `return` with no expression after it, the function returns `None`.

## Default values and keyword arguments

You can specify default values for parameters in your function definition. This allows callers to omit arguments when invoking the function.

```python
def make_coffee(style="black", cups=1):
    """Print coffee preparation details."""
    print(f"Preparing {cups} cup(s) of {style} coffee.")
```

When calling a function, arguments can be supplied positionally (mapped by order) or by keyword using `parameter_name=value`. Positional arguments must always come before any keyword arguments:

```python
# Using defaults
make_coffee()

# Overriding by position
make_coffee("latte", 2)

# Using keyword arguments
make_coffee(cups=3, style="espresso")
```

Note that PEP 8 recommends using no spaces around the `=` sign when defining default parameter values or passing keyword arguments. Additionally, default values are evaluated only once when the function is defined, so mutable objects like lists should generally be avoided as default values.

## Understanding variable scope

Variables created inside a function have local scope. They exist only while the function is running and cannot be accessed outside of it. Conversely, variables created outside functions have global scope and can be accessed anywhere in the program.

```python
def show_count():
    local_count = 10
    print(local_count)

show_count()
# local_count no longer exists out here
```

Restricting variables to local scope keeps your code modular and prevents accidental modifications from elsewhere in your program.

### Try it

Write a function called `calculate_total` that accepts a required `price` and an optional `tax_rate` with a default value of `0.20`. Have it return the total amount (price plus price multiplied by tax rate). Test calling the function first with just the price, and then with a custom tax rate passed as a keyword argument.

### Key points

- Define a function using the `def` keyword, a name, parentheses for parameters, and an indented body.
- A docstring directly below the `def` line documents the purpose of the function.
- The `return` statement sends a value back to the caller; functions without a `return` evaluate to `None`.
- Default parameter values make arguments optional, and function calls can mix positional and keyword arguments as long as positional arguments come first.
- Variables created inside a function belong to the local scope and disappear once the function completes execution.

python-for-everyone/3/2.body:
In this lesson, you will learn how to open files on your computer, read text from them in different ways, and write or append new data safely.

## Opening and closing files

To interact with a file in Python, you use the built-in `open()` function. This function returns a file object and typically takes two arguments: the filename and the mode. The mode specifies how you intend to use the file:

- `'r'`: Read mode. This is the default if you omit the mode argument. It opens an existing file for reading; if the file does not exist, an error occurs.
- `'w'`: Write mode. This opens a file for writing. If the file already exists, its contents are erased. If it does not exist, Python creates it.
- `'a'`: Append mode. This opens a file to add data to the end without deleting existing contents.

It is best practice to open files using the `with` statement. The `with` block guarantees that the file is properly closed when the block finishes, even if an error occurs. If you do not use `with`, you must call `close()` on the file object manually so buffered changes are saved to disk.

```python
with open('notes.txt', 'w') as file:
    file.write('First entry\n')
```

## Reading data from a file

Python provides several ways to read text from an open file:

- `read()`: Reads the whole file (or a specified number of characters) and returns it as a single string. It returns an empty string when it reaches the end of the file.
- `readline()`: Reads a single line at a time, keeping the newline character (`\n`) at the end.
- `readlines()`: Reads all lines into a list of strings.

You can also iterate over the file object directly using a `for` loop. This approach is fast, memory efficient, and easy to read.

```python
with open('notes.txt', 'r') as file:
    for line in file:
        print(line, end='')
```

## Writing text to a file

The `write()` method takes a string and writes it to the file. Unlike the `print()` function, `write()` does not automatically add a newline character (`\n`) to the end of your text, so you must add one explicitly if you want subsequent text on a new line.

The `write()` method only accepts strings. If you want to write numbers, tuples, or other types, convert them to a string first using `str()`.

```python
items = [10, 20, 30]

with open('numbers.txt', 'w') as file:
    for item in items:
        file.write(str(item) + '\n')
```

### Try it

Write a short Python script that opens a file called `todo.txt` in append mode (`'a'`). Write two tasks to the file, making sure each task ends with a newline (`\n`). Then, open the file in read mode and print each line using a `for` loop.

### Key points

- The `open()` function takes a filename and an optional mode string such as `'r'`, `'w'`, or `'a'`.
- Using a `with` statement automatically closes the file when the block ends, ensuring all data is written to disk.
- You can read file contents using `read()`, `readline()`, `readlines()`, or by looping directly over the file object.
- The `write()` method accepts only strings and does not insert newlines automatically.

python-for-everyone/3/3.body:
In this project, you will combine functions, file input and output, and user input to build a small command-line journal application. By the end, you will have a working program that appends new thoughts to a persistent file and prints previous entries back to your screen.

## Step 1: Writing new entries

A journal needs a way to save new thoughts without wiping away previous entries. In Python, you can open a file in append mode by supplying `'a'` as the second argument to `open()`. Any string written with `write()` will be added to the end of the file.

Wrapping this behaviour in a dedicated function keeps your code tidy and reusable:

```python
def record_entry(entry_text, filename="journal.txt"):
    """Append a new entry to the chosen journal file."""
    with open(filename, "a") as file_obj:
        file_obj.write(entry_text + "\n")
```

Using the `with` statement ensures Python closes the file properly once the block finishes, even if an error occurs. Setting a default argument for `filename` lets you call `record_entry("Learned about files")` without repeating the file path each time.

## Step 2: Reading previous entries

Next, the journal needs a way to display existing entries. You can open a file in read mode (`'r'`), which is also the default mode when you omit the second argument from `open()`.

To display each line cleanly, you can loop directly over the file object:

```python
def show_journal(filename="journal.txt"):
    """Read and display all entries from the journal file."""
    with open(filename, "r") as file_obj:
        print("--- Your Journal Entries ---")
        for line in file_obj:
            print(line, end="")
        print("----------------------------")
```

Looping directly over `file_obj` is memory efficient, fast, and leads to simple code. Specifying `end=""` inside `print()` prevents duplicate empty lines, since each line already ends with a newline character (`\n`).

## Step 3: Creating an interactive menu

Now you can tie both functions together using a loop and `input()`. This lets the user choose whether to write a new note, read past notes, or exit the program.

```python
def run_journal():
    """Run the interactive journal application."""
    while True:
        print("\n1. Add an entry")
        print("2. Read all entries")
        print("3. Quit")
        choice = input("Select an option (1-3): ")

        if choice == "1":
            thought = input("Write your entry: ")
            record_entry(thought)
            print("Entry saved.")
        elif choice == "2":
            show_journal()
        elif choice == "3":
            print("Goodbye!")
            break
        else:
            print("Unrecognised option. Please choose 1, 2, or 3.")

run_journal()
```

The `while True` loop keeps asking for instructions until the user inputs `"3"`, which executes the `break` statement to exit the loop.

### Try it

Create a file named `my_journal.py` with the code above and run it. Add two different entries through the menu, exit the program, and then restart it. Choose option `2` to confirm that your entries remained saved on disk.

### Key points

- Open files in append mode (`'a'`) to add text to the end of a file without overwriting existing data.
- Wrap file operations in functions to organise your code and assign helpful default parameter values.
- Use `with open(...)` to make sure files are closed promptly and safely.
- Loop directly over a file object (`for line in file:`) to read text efficiently line by line.

By the end of this lesson, you will be able to import pandas, create its two primary data structures—the Series and the DataFrame—and run basic methods to inspect your data.

## Importing pandas and creating a DataFrame

To begin using pandas, import the library using the standard community alias, `pd`:

```python
import pandas as pd
```

A `DataFrame` is a two-dimensional, labelled data structure with columns that can hold different data types, such as integers, floats, and strings. You can think of it as a spreadsheet table or a SQL table. One common way to create a `DataFrame` manually is by passing a Python dictionary of lists to the constructor. The dictionary keys become the column headers, and the list values become the column contents:

```python
df = pd.DataFrame({
    "Name": ["Braund, Mr. Owen Harris", "Allen, Mr. William Henry", "Bonnell, Miss Elizabeth"],
    "Age": [22, 35, 58],
    "Sex": ["male", "male", "female"],
})
```

The resulting table has three labelled columns (`Name`, `Age`, and `Sex`). By default, pandas assigns an integer index to label the rows, beginning at 0.

## Understanding the Series

While a `DataFrame` represents a full two-dimensional table, each individual column within that table is a `Series`. A `Series` is a one-dimensional labelled array. You can extract a single column from a `DataFrame` using square brackets with the column label, similar to accessing a value by key in a Python dictionary:

```python
ages = df["Age"]
```

This selection yields a `Series`. You can also instantiate a `Series` directly from a list or array, optionally providing a `name` parameter:

```python
ages = pd.Series([22, 35, 58], name="Age")
```

A `Series` does not have column labels because it holds only a single column, but it retains row labels via its index.

## Calling methods on DataFrames and Series

pandas provides methods to perform calculations and data transformations. Because these are methods, you execute them using parentheses `()`.

For example, you can calculate the highest value in a numerical `Series` or column by calling `.max()`:

```python
# Called on a DataFrame column
max_age = df["Age"].max()

# Called on an independent Series
max_age = ages.max()
```

To inspect summary figures for all numerical columns in a `DataFrame`, call the `.describe()` method:

```python
df.describe()
```

The `.describe()` method provides a quick overview of the numerical data in a `DataFrame`. Because columns such as `Name` and `Sex` contain textual data, they are not taken into account by `.describe()` by default.

### Try it

Create a new Python script or interactive session and complete the following:

1. Import pandas as `pd`.
2. Create a `DataFrame` with two columns: `"Product"` containing three product names as strings, and `"Price"` containing three float values.
3. Extract the `"Price"` column into a variable.
4. Call `.max()` on your price variable to find the highest price, and run `.describe()` on the entire `DataFrame`.

### Key points

- The standard convention to load pandas is `import pandas as pd`.
- A `DataFrame` is a two-dimensional labelled data structure capable of holding multiple data types in its columns.
- Each column of a `DataFrame` is a one-dimensional labelled array called a `Series`.
- Square bracket notation (`df["col_name"]`) selects a single column as a `Series`.
- You can perform calculations and summaries by invoking methods such as `.max()` and `.describe()`.

data-analysis-pandas/1/2.title: Reading CSV files
data-analysis-pandas/1/2.body:
You will be able to import tabular text data into pandas using `pd.read_csv()`, configure column names and row indices, select specific subsets of columns, and control data types and missing values.

## Loading flat files and custom delimiters

The primary tool for loading delimited text data in pandas is the `read_csv()` function. By default, it expects comma-separated values, but you can customise the delimiter with the `sep` parameter.

```python
import pandas as pd
from io import StringIO

data = """id,item,price
101,apples,2.50
102,oranges,3.10
"""

df = pd.read_csv(StringIO(data))
print(df)
```

If your file uses a different delimiter, such as a pipe or tab, provide it using `sep="|"`. You can also let pandas detect delimiters automatically by setting `sep=None`, which uses Python's built-in sniffer tool via `engine="python"`.

## Configuring headers, columns, and index labels

By default, `read_csv()` treats the first line of data as the header containing column names (`header="infer"`). When a file lacks column headers, set `header=None` and supply an explicit list of column labels to the `names` parameter:

```python
raw_data = """101,apples,2.50
102,oranges,3.10
"""

df = pd.read_csv(StringIO(raw_data), header=None, names=["id", "item", "price"])
```

You can designate one or more columns as the DataFrame row labels using `index_col`:

- Setting `index_col="id"` or `index_col=0` uses that column as the row index.
- Supplying a list of column numbers or names, such as `index_col=[0, 1]`, constructs a hierarchical MultiIndex.
- Passing `index_col=False` prevents pandas from using the first column as the index when trailing delimiters confuse line parsing.

To reduce memory usage and parsing time on wide datasets, use `usecols` to load only the required columns. It accepts column names, positional integer indices, or a callable function:

```python
df_sub = pd.read_csv(StringIO(data), usecols=["item", "price"])
```

## Parsing data types, dates, and missing values

pandas infers column data types automatically, but you can explicitly specify them with the `dtype` parameter by passing a type or a dictionary mapping column names to types:

```python
df = pd.read_csv(StringIO(data), dtype={"id": "Int64", "price": float})
```

You can also pass `dtype="category"` or a dictionary mapping specific columns to `"category"` to parse categorical variables directly.

When dealing with date and time columns:

- Pass a list of column names or positions to `parse_dates` to convert them into datetime objects.
- Use `date_format` to define an explicit datetime format string, or pass `dayfirst=True` when reading international DD/MM/YYYY formats.

Missing values are converted to `NaN` by default. You can define additional representations using `na_values`, such as `na_values=["missing", "0"]`. If you want only your specified values to be treated as missing without including the default strings (such as `'NA'`, `'NaN'`, and empty strings), set `keep_default_na=False`.

### Try it

Suppose you receive sensor readings where lines beginning with `#` are comments, dates are formatted as day-first, and missing numbers are marked as `None`:

```python
sensor_data = """# Daily sensor output
reading_id,timestamp,value
1,15/04/2024,24.5
2,16/04/2024,None
3,17/04/2024,25.1
"""

df = pd.read_csv(
    StringIO(sensor_data),
    comment="#",
    index_col="reading_id",
    parse_dates=["timestamp"],
    dayfirst=True,
    na_values=["None"],
)
print(df)
print(df.dtypes)
```

Run this snippet and inspect the DataFrame index, column data types, and how the missing entry is converted into `NaN`.

### Key points

- Load delimited files into a DataFrame using `pd.read_csv()`, adjusting delimiters with `sep`.
- Set `header=None` and pass `names` when the file lacks column headers, or choose row labels with `index_col`.
- Restrict parsed columns using `usecols` to minimise memory consumption and speed up processing.
- Control type conversion with `dtype`, convert dates using `parse_dates` and `date_format`, and customise missing values with `na_values` and `keep_default_na`.

data-analysis-pandas/1/3.title: Exploring a DataFrame
data-analysis-pandas/1/3.body:
Once you load a dataset into a pandas DataFrame, the first step is to explore its structure, dimensions, and contents. You will learn how to inspect row samples, verify table dimensions, check column data types, and produce descriptive summary statistics.

## Viewing samples and dimensions

To inspect a small sample of your data without printing the entire table, use the `head()` and `tail()` methods. By default, both methods display five rows, but you can pass an integer argument to view a custom number of rows from the start or end of the DataFrame:

```python
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({
    "name": ["Alice", "Bob", "Charlie", "David", "Eva", "Frank"],
    "age": [24, 30, 22, 35, 29, 41],
    "salary": [48000, 52000, 45000, 61000, 58000, 72000]
})

df.head(3)
df.tail(2)
```

To find the dimensions of your DataFrame, access the `shape` attribute. Because `shape` is an attribute rather than a method, do not use parentheses. It returns a tuple in the format `(nrows, ncolumns)`:

```python
df.shape
```

You can also inspect axis labels directly via the `index` (row labels) and `columns` (column labels) attributes.

## Checking column types and filtering by dtype

A DataFrame can store columns of varying types, such as integers, floating-point numbers, and strings. You can inspect the data type of every column using the `dtypes` attribute, which returns a Series:

```python
df.dtypes
```

To see a count of how many columns belong to each data type, call `value_counts()` on the attribute:

```python
df.dtypes.value_counts()
```

When dealing with many columns, you can isolate specific types using `select_dtypes()`. This method accepts `include` and `exclude` parameters:

```python
# Select only numeric columns
numeric_df = df.select_dtypes(include=["number"])

# Select string columns
string_df = df.select_dtypes(include=[str])
```

## Summarising data with descriptive statistics

The `describe()` method calculates a set of summary statistics across the columns of a DataFrame, such as count, mean, standard deviation, minimum, maximum, and percentiles:

```python
df.describe()
```

On a DataFrame with mixed data types, `describe()` restricts the output by default to numerical columns. If no numerical columns exist, it summarises categorical columns. You can alter this behaviour using the `include` parameter. For instance, `df.describe(include="all")` includes all columns in the summary.

For categorical or discrete fields, use `value_counts()` on a column to calculate frequency counts:

```python
df["age"].value_counts()
```

To find the number of unique non-null observations in a column, call `nunique()`:

```python
df["age"].nunique()
```

### Try it

Create a DataFrame containing five passenger records with columns `"name"` (strings), `"age"` (integers), and `"survived"` (booleans). Use `shape` to verify that there are 5 rows and 3 columns, view the last 3 rows with `tail(3)`, and print summary statistics for all columns using `describe(include="all")`.

### Key points

- Use `head()` and `tail()` to display a sample of rows from the beginning or end of a DataFrame, defaulting to five rows.
- Access the `shape` attribute (without parentheses) to retrieve a tuple of `(nrows, ncolumns)`.
- Inspect column data types using the `dtypes` attribute and subset columns based on type with `select_dtypes()`.
- Compute quick summary metrics across numeric columns using `describe()`, or use `describe(include="all")` for full coverage.

data-analysis-pandas/2/1.title: Missing values
data-analysis-pandas/2/1.body:
In this lesson, you will learn how pandas represents missing data across different data types, how missing values behave in calculations, and how to detect, drop, fill, and interpolate them in your datasets.

## Missing value sentinels and detection

pandas uses different sentinel markers to represent missing data depending on the column data type:

- `np.nan` represents missing values in NumPy data types. Using it often coerces integers or booleans to `np.float64` or `object`.
- `pd.NaT` represents missing values in datetime, timedelta, and period types.
- `pd.NA` is a dedicated scalar indicator for nullable types, such as `Int64`, `Float64`, `StringDtype`, and `ArrowDtype`. These preserve the underlying data type.

To check for missing values, use `isna()` or `notna()`. You must avoid checking for missing data using standard equality comparisons (`==`), because `np.nan == np.nan` evaluates to `False`, while `pd.NA == pd.NA` returns `pd.NA`:

```python
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np

ser = pd.Series([1, None, 3], dtype="Int64")
print(ser.isna())
print(ser == pd.NA)
```

To convert a DataFrame containing `np.nan` into nullable data types that use `pd.NA`, use `convert_dtypes()`.

## Behaviour in calculations

In arithmetic operations, missing values propagate: operating on an unknown value results in an unknown value (such as `pd.NA + 1` returning `<NA>`). In logical operations (`&`, `|`), `pd.NA` follows three-valued Kleene logic. It only propagates if the outcome cannot be known beforehand (for example, `True | pd.NA` evaluates to `True`, whereas `False | pd.NA` evaluates to `<NA>`).

Because `bool(pd.NA)` raises a `TypeError`, you cannot evaluate `pd.NA` in a standard Python `if` statement or use Python's `and`, `or`, and `not` keywords. Use the bitwise operators `&`, `|`, and `~` instead.

Unlike NumPy, pandas reductions such as `mean()`, `std()`, and `sum()` skip missing values by default (`skipna=True`). When summing, NA values or entirely empty data evaluate to 0, while `prod()` evaluates to 1:

```python
s = pd.Series([1.0, np.nan, 3.0])
print(s.std())              # Skips missing values
print(s.std(skipna=False))  # Returns NaN
```

## Dropping, filling, and interpolating

To discard missing entries, call `dropna()`. By default, this drops rows containing NA values, but setting `axis=1` drops columns instead.

To fill missing values with non-NA values, use `fillna()`:

```python
df = pd.DataFrame({
    "A": [1.0, np.nan, 3.0],
    "B": [np.nan, 2.0, 4.0]
})

# Fill with a scalar
filled_scalar = df.fillna(0)

# Fill per column with a dictionary or column means
filled_mean = df.fillna(df.mean())
```

You can also propagate neighbouring values using `ffill()` (forward fill) or `bfill()` (backward fill). Both methods accept a `limit` parameter to constrain how many consecutive gaps are filled.

For continuous series, `interpolate()` estimates missing points based on nearby observations. It defaults to linear interpolation, but you can set `method="time"` for time series, `method="values"` for floating-point indices, or specify SciPy methods like `"pchip"` or `"barycentric"`:

```python
ser = pd.Series([1.0, np.nan, 5.0, np.nan, 9.0])
print(ser.interpolate(limit=1))
```

### Try it

Create a pandas Series with values `[10, np.nan, np.nan, 40]` using `dtype="Int64"`. Use `isna()` to display the missing mask, fill the first missing entry only using forward fill with a limit of 1, and then verify the remaining missing count using `sum()` on `isna()`.

### Key points

- pandas uses `np.nan` for NumPy types, `pd.NaT` for datetime types, and `pd.NA` for nullable extension types.
- Always detect missing entries with `isna()` or `notna()` rather than equality operators (`==`).
- Reduction methods such as `sum()` and `mean()` exclude missing entries by default using `skipna=True`.
- You can clean missing data using `dropna()` to remove entries, `fillna()` to replace values, or `interpolate()` to estimate values across gaps.

data-analysis-pandas/2/2.title: Fixing types and dates
data-analysis-pandas/2/2.body:
In this lesson, you will learn how to convert raw string and numerical values into proper pandas datetime objects, handle invalid date values safely, and access date components for analysis.

## Converting values to timestamps

When importing data from formats like CSV, dates are frequently read as plain text objects. In plain text format, you cannot perform calendar operations, extract months, or calculate intervals. The primary tool for fixing this is `pd.to_datetime`.

Applying `pd.to_datetime` converts text series into datetime objects (with a `datetime64[us]` data type by default):

```python
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({
    "recorded_at": ["2024-03-15 08:30", "2024-03-16 09:45", "2024-03-17 11:15"],
    "value": [12.4, 15.1, 9.8]
})

df["recorded_at"] = pd.to_datetime(df["recorded_at"])
print(df["recorded_at"].dtype)
```

You can also convert dates during import by passing `parse_dates=["recorded_at"]` to functions such as `pd.read_csv`.

## Handling formats, day-first dates, and errors

Date strings come in varied structures. When parsing non-standard strings, specify the expected structure with the `format` argument to ensure precise and faster parsing. If your dates use day-first formatting (such as European `DD/MM/YYYY`), pass `dayfirst=True`:

```python
# Using dayfirst for European dates
eu_dates = pd.Series(["15/03/2024", "16/03/2024"])
pd.to_datetime(eu_dates, dayfirst=True)

# Using explicit format patterns
pd.to_datetime(pd.Series(["2024/03/15"]), format="%Y/%m/%d")
```

Real-world data often includes corrupt or unparseable text. By default, `pd.to_datetime` raises an exception if a value cannot be parsed (`errors="raise"`). Setting `errors="coerce"` converts invalid entries into `pd.NaT` (Not a Time), which is the missing-value marker for date data:

```python
mixed_series = pd.Series(["2024-01-01", "invalid_date", "2024-01-03"])
clean_dates = pd.to_datetime(mixed_series, errors="coerce")
print(clean_dates)
```

pandas can also assemble datetime values across separate DataFrame columns when given columns such as `year`, `month`, and `day`:

```python
parts = pd.DataFrame({"year": [2024, 2024], "month": [1, 2], "day": [15, 20]})
assembled = pd.to_datetime(parts)
```

## Using the .dt accessor and date arithmetic

Once a column has a datetime type, its individual components become accessible through the `.dt` accessor. Properties include `.dt.year`, `.dt.month`, `.dt.day`, `.dt.hour`, and `.dt.day_of_week` (where Monday is 0 and Sunday is 6):

```python
df["month"] = df["recorded_at"].dt.month
df["weekday"] = df["recorded_at"].dt.day_of_week
```

Datetime objects also support direct mathematical operations. Subtracting two timestamps returns a `pd.Timedelta` object, which defines a precise time duration:

```python
duration = df["recorded_at"].max() - df["recorded_at"].min()
print(duration)
```

## DatetimeIndex and slicing

When a datetime column is moved to the index (using `.set_index`), the object becomes a `DatetimeIndex`. In addition to making `.dt` properties available directly on the index (such as `df.index.year`), this allows partial string slicing:

```python
df = df.set_index("recorded_at")
subset = df["2024-03-15":"2024-03-16"]
```

Unlike standard Python slicing, label-based slicing on a `DatetimeIndex` includes both endpoints.

### Try it

Create a DataFrame with three messy string dates (including one invalid string such as `"missing"`) and a numerical column. Use `pd.to_datetime` with `errors="coerce"` to transform the dates, extract the day of the week into a new column with `.dt.day_of_week`, and verify that the invalid entry is represented as `NaT`.

### Key points

- Convert text or integer columns to datetime objects using `pd.to_datetime` or the `parse_dates` argument in file readers.
- Use `dayfirst=True` or provide an explicit `format` string to resolve ambiguous dates.
- Pass `errors="coerce"` to replace unparseable strings with `NaT` instead of halting execution.
- Access calendar properties like month, year, and weekday using the `.dt` accessor on Series, or directly on a `DatetimeIndex`.
- Subtracting timestamps yields a `Timedelta` duration object, and slicing a `DatetimeIndex` includes both endpoints.
